summary: Antioch on the Orontes: a great city of the Roman east and seat of a patriarch, fought over by Persians, Arabs and Byzantines, taken by the First Crusade in 1098 as the capital of a Norman principality, and destroyed by Baybars in 1268.
overview: Antioch was the key to northern Syria, the city that controlled the road between Anatolia and Aleppo. It changed hands between Persia, the caliphate, the Byzantine Empire, the Seljuks and the crusaders, was the scene of the longest and most famous siege of the First Crusade, and after its destruction by the Mamluks in 1268 shrank to a small town inside its ruined walls.
knownFor: One of the great cities of the Roman east and seat of an ancient patriarchate
Byzantine recovery in 969 after more than three centuries of Muslim rule
The crusader siege of 1097–1098 and the defeat of Kerbogha
Capital of the Norman principality of Antioch, 1098–1268
Walls climbing Mount Silpius, and destruction by Baybars in 1268

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Antioch stands on the Orontes where the river passes between the ridge of Mount Silpius and the plain of the Amuq, on the road from Anatolia through the Syrian Gates to Aleppo. The position made it a prize for a thousand years: it fell to a Persian king in 540, to the Arabs in the 630s, to a Byzantine commander in 969, to the Seljuks in 1084 and to the First Crusade in 1098, and the Mamluk sultan Baybars destroyed it in 1268.

Its medieval story is one of a shrinking population inside enormous walls, a circuit over Mount Silpius so long that in both 969 and 1098 the city fell to attackers who got over a thinly held stretch of it.

contentSections.title: Late antique Antioch
paragraphs: Founded by Seleucus I in about 300 BC, Antioch became the capital of Roman Syria and, by most estimates, the third city of the empire. The Acts of the Apostles records that the followers of Jesus were first called Christians there, and its bishop ranked among the five patriarchs of the early Church.

The sixth century broke it. An earthquake in 526 killed a very large number of people (the chronicler John Malalas gives 250,000, usually treated as an exaggeration), and in 540 the Sasanian king Khosrow I stormed and burned the city and deported its people to a new town near Ctesiphon. Justinian I rebuilt the walls, according to Procopius on a shorter line, but Antioch never regained its ancient size.

contentSections.title: Persians, Arabs and the frontier, 540–969
paragraphs: Persian armies held Antioch again for most of the years between 611 and 628, and within a decade the Arabs arrived: after Abu Ubayda defeated the Byzantines at the Iron Bridge over the Orontes in 637, the city surrendered on terms. Under the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs it was a frontier town facing the Taurus passes, still largely Christian, while the Melkite and Syriac Orthodox patriarchs who claimed its see often lived elsewhere.

In the 940s the Hamdanid emir Sayf al-Dawla made Aleppo the base of his wars against the Byzantine Empire, with Antioch under his rule, and the conquest of Cilicia by Nikephoros II in 964–965 opened the road to the city.

contentSections.title: The Byzantine duchy, 969–1084
paragraphs: Nikephoros blockaded Antioch from a fort at Baghras and forbade an assault, wanting a working provincial capital rather than a ruin. On the night of 28 October 969 Michael Bourtzes disobeyed him, seized two towers with about three hundred men and held them for three days until the army arrived. After Nikephoros was murdered in December, with Bourtzes among the conspirators, John I Tzimiskes made Bourtzes the first doux of Antioch.

For 115 years the duchy anchored the empire's eastern frontier, its dukes commanding the small themes of Cilicia and northern Syria and treating Aleppo as a tributary. Melkite Christians from Fatimid Egypt settled in the city, among them the chronicler Yahya of Antioch. After the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 the Armenian general Philaretos Brachamios held Antioch as a nearly independent lord, until Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, the Seljuk ruler of Rum, took it by surprise in December 1084.

contentSections.title: The First Crusade, 1097–1098
paragraphs: From 1086 Antioch was held by Yaghi-Siyan, a Turkish governor for the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I, who ruled it almost independently after 1092. The First Crusade arrived on 21 October 1097, and the siege dragged through a winter of famine. The city fell by treachery: Bohemond of Taranto won over Firuz, a tower commander, and on the night of 2–3 June 1098 the crusaders climbed in by his tower and massacred the Muslim inhabitants, though the citadel held out.

Within days Kerbogha, atabeg of Mosul, arrived and besieged the besiegers. Stephen-Henry, Count of Blois, who had deserted on 2 June, persuaded Alexios I Komnenos to turn his relief army back. The starving crusaders were rallied by the discovery in the cathedral of St Peter of a spearhead that the visionary Peter Bartholomew said had pierced Christ's side, and on 28 June they marched out and routed Kerbogha's divided army. Bohemond then claimed the city: the papal legate Adhemar of Le Puy died there on 1 August, Raymond IV of Toulouse could not dislodge Bohemond, and the oath to restore Antioch to Alexios was never kept.

contentSections.title: The principality of Antioch, 1098–1268
paragraphs: Bohemond's principality was the most Norman of the crusader states. While he was a prisoner of the Danishmend Turks in 1100–1103, and after he left for Italy, his nephew Tancred governed. Defeated at Dyrrachium, Bohemond accepted the Treaty of Devol in 1108 as the emperor's vassal, but Tancred ignored it. A Latin patriarch had replaced the Greek one in 1100, and the Byzantine claim to the city shaped imperial policy for the rest of the century.

After Roger of Salerno was killed at the Field of Blood in 1119, Baldwin II of Jerusalem governed as regent. The heiress Constance's first husband, Raymond of Poitou, did homage to John II Komnenos before the walls in 1137 and was killed by Nur ad-Din at Inab in 1149; her second, Reynald of Châtillon, raided Byzantine Cyprus and had to walk beside the emperor's horse when Manuel I Komnenos rode into Antioch in state at Easter 1159. The city stayed Latin after the Battle of Hattin in 1187, but a long succession war after 1201 between Bohemond IV of Tripoli and the Armenian-backed Raymond-Roupen left it weak, and in 1260 Bohemond VI submitted to the Mongols.

contentSections.title: Baybars and the fall of 1268
paragraphs: The Mamluks punished that alliance in May 1268. With Bohemond VI away at Tripoli and too few men to hold the walls, Antioch was stormed on 18 May, and those who had fled to the citadel surrendered two days later. Baybars had the population killed or enslaved and the churches of St Peter and St Paul burned, and sent Bohemond a letter by his secretary Ibn Abd al-Zahir describing the slaughter. Later chroniclers gave 17,000 dead and 100,000 captives, figures that cannot be checked; the historian Thomas Madden has called it the greatest single massacre of the crusading era.

Antioch never recovered. Under the Mamluks it was a small district town governed from Aleppo, and by 1432, according to a figure repeated in modern histories, only about three hundred houses inside the walls were occupied. The Ottomans took it with the rest of Syria in 1516.

contentSections.title: Rulers and notable figures
paragraphs: The Byzantine century runs from Michael Bourtzes, conqueror and twice doux, to Philaretos Brachamios, who lost the city to the Seljuks. Bohemond I of Antioch founded the principality by refusing to surrender the city; Bohemond II of Antioch, killed in Cilicia in 1130, left only a small daughter, Constance; and her son Bohemond III reigned for almost forty years.

Among its enemies, Kerbogha lost his army before its walls, Nur ad-Din killed one prince at Inab and captured another at Harim in 1164, and Baybars ended its history as a great city. Yahya of Antioch chronicled the Byzantine city from within, and an anonymous knight in Bohemond's following wrote the Gesta Francorum, the crusader camp's account of the siege.

contentSections.title: The medieval city
paragraphs: The walls were Antioch's great monument. The circuit ran along the Orontes on the west and climbed the ridge of Silpius on the east to take in the summit citadel, and crusader writers counted about four hundred towers. In a ravine on the mountainside the Iron Gate, a dam-wall probably of Justinian's time, held back the torrent that ran down through the town. The crusaders named the main gates: the Bridge Gate toward the port of St Symeon at the mouth of the Orontes, the Gate of St Paul on the Aleppo road, and the Gate of St George to the south.

Inside, the inhabited town shrank toward the river. The cathedral of St Peter, seat of the Latin patriarchs, stood in the lower town, and a cave church on the slope outside, traditionally founded by the apostle Peter, remained a place of pilgrimage. Genoese merchants received a quarter from Bohemond in 1098, and Pisans and Venetians later won privileges. The Habib-i Neccar mosque, by tradition a church converted after the Arab conquest, still stands in Antakya.

contentSections.title: Antioch beyond its walls
paragraphs: The title outlived the city. Five churches still call their patriarchs 'of Antioch', although none has resided there since the Middle Ages, and the Latin patriarchate founded in 1100 survived as a papal title until 1964. The siege of 1097–1098 became the central epic of the First Crusade, retold in the Gesta Francorum and the Old French Chanson d'Antioche, while Bohemond's refusal to hand the city back soured Byzantine relations with the crusaders for a century. Its fall in 1268 exposed the crusader coast to the Mamluk conquests that ended with the fall of Acre in 1291.

timeline.title: Founded
timeline.description: Seleucus I founds the city on the Orontes as a Seleucid capital.

timeline.title: Earthquake
timeline.description: A catastrophic earthquake kills a large part of the population.

timeline.title: Sacked by Khosrow I
timeline.description: The Sasanian king storms the city and deports its people to a new settlement near Ctesiphon.

timeline.title: Arab conquest
timeline.description: After the Byzantine defeat at the Iron Bridge the city surrenders on terms, and stays in Muslim hands for over three centuries.

timeline.title: Recovered by the Byzantines
timeline.description: Michael Bourtzes takes the walls by escalade against the emperor's orders.

timeline.title: Taken by Suleiman ibn Qutalmish
timeline.description: The Seljuk ruler of Rum surprises the city and ends the Byzantine duchy.

timeline.title: The crusaders arrive
timeline.description: The First Crusade begins its eight-month siege.

timeline.title: The city falls
timeline.description: Firuz lets the crusaders in by his tower; Kerbogha arrives days later.

timeline.title: Kerbogha defeated
timeline.description: The crusaders march out behind the newly found relic and rout the relieving army.

timeline.title: Treaty of Devol
timeline.description: Bohemond agrees to hold Antioch as a vassal of Alexios I; Tancred ignores the treaty.

timeline.title: The Field of Blood
timeline.description: Roger of Salerno is killed with most of his army, and Baldwin II of Jerusalem becomes regent.

timeline.title: Manuel I enters in state
timeline.description: Reynald of Châtillon walks beside the emperor's horse as the principality accepts Byzantine overlordship.

timeline.title: Destroyed by Baybars
timeline.description: The Mamluk sultan storms the city, kills or enslaves its people and burns its churches.

timeline.title: Ottoman conquest
timeline.description: Antioch passes to the Ottomans with the rest of Syria.
